_README: Copy this file, rename it, and fill it in. This is the ONLY file you edit
to change what a video looks like or who is in it - no module needs
touching. Delete the _README and _hint keys when you are done; anything
starting with an underscore is ignored.
That generates every sprite once. Later videos using this cast composite
the same PNGs and generate nothing, which is what stops characters
drifting from one video to the next.
Check it first:  python scripts/build.py --check  (validates every cast)
name: my_cast
_hint_name: Lowercase, no spaces. Names the sprite folder: casts/<name>/sprites/
description: One line on what this cast is for and who plays what.
style: REPLACE ME - the art direction, applied to every generated image
_hint_style: The single most important field. Name a specific, recognisable look and
the drawing technique, not a mood. Include line weight and shading.
Good:  'Studio Ghibli watercolour background art style, soft gouache
washes, visible paper grain, gentle outlines, muted palette'

background.prompt: REPLACE ME - the one plate every shot sits on

_hint_background: Worth more time than anything else here: the horizon decides whether
characters look planted or adrift. Say three things explicitly -
1. where the horizon sits ('low horizon two thirds down the frame')
2. that the middle is empty ('wide open empty middle with nothing in it')
3. that the edges stay clear (scenery 'only at the extreme left and
right edges', 'no taller than a quarter of the image')
Tall scenery at the edges frames the shot and makes every character look
small and lost. Ask for an empty stage, not a nice picture.

hero.role: what this character MEANS in the argument, not who they are
hero._hint_role: e.g. 'the boss and the capital', 'asks the naive question'. The director casts from these.
hero.look: REPLACE ME - the character's fixed appearance, repeated in every pose
_hint_look: Written once, prepended to every pose prompt. Be exhaustive and
concrete: body shape, colours, clothing, distinguishing features.
Anything vague here drifts differently in each pose.
_hint_relative_height: Height relative to the other characters, 0.3-3.0. Pick one character
as 1.0 and size the rest against them. The director sets one height
per shot and cannot keep the cast in proportion across shots; this
makes the relationship a fact of the cast instead.

poses.stand: standing upright facing the viewer, neutral expression
poses.point: standing and pointing forward with one raised hand, explaining
poses.think: standing with a hand on the chin, considering something
poses.happy: standing with both arms raised, delighted

_hint_poses: Aim for 8-10 per main character. Four is enough to work and few
enough to see repeats across fifteen shots. Describe the BODY, not
the scene - no props, no floor, no background; those are separate
sprites the director places beside the character.

props.example_object: a single plain object, described concretely, seen from the front

_hint_props: Each is ONE inanimate object. The generator is already told 'no
characters, no hands' because asked for 'a stack of plates' in a
character style it helpfully draws someone holding them - and a prop
with a character baked in puts that character on screen twice.
Include a few blank surfaces - a whiteboard, a card, a signpost. Text is
drawn over them with PIL, which is always correct, whereas asking the
image model for Chinese text gives you plausible-looking nonsense.
_hint_hanging: Prop names (without the prop_ prefix) that hang at eye level: boards,
charts, maps, clocks, signage. Everything not listed is put on the
ground whatever the director asks for, because left to itself a director
will hang a pile of gold coins at eye level like a wall chart.
_hint_foreground: Prop names that draw OVER the characters: tables, counters, sinks, desks
- anything a character stands or works behind. This overlap is most of
what makes a shot read as a scene rather than as cut-outs side by side.
